tips.title: Like terms match letter and power
tips.body: $3x$ and $5x$ are like terms. $3x$ and $3x^2$ are **not** — same letter, different power. Neither are $3x$ and $3y$. Only like terms can be collected, so check **both** the letter and the power before adding anything.

tips.title: The sign belongs to the term after it
tips.body: In $7x - 4x + 2$, the terms are $+7x$, $-4x$ and $+2$. Reading the sign as part of the term that follows it removes almost every sign error in collecting terms.

tips.title: Substitute a number to check an expansion
tips.body: Put $x = 2$ into the original and into your answer. If they disagree, the expansion is wrong. It takes seconds and catches a sign slip that staring at the algebra will not. Avoid $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, which hide too much.

tips.title: Multiply every term inside the bracket
tips.body: In $3(2x + 5)$ the 3 multiplies **both** the $2x$ **and** the $5$. Forgetting the second term is the commonest expansion error, and it is why writing the two products separately before adding is worth the extra line.

tips.title: Factorising is expanding backwards
tips.body: To factorise, find the **highest common factor** and take it outside. Always check by **expanding back**: $4(3x + 5) = 12x + 20$. If it does not return the original, the factor taken out was not the highest, or a sign is wrong.

why.matters:
Two expressions can look nothing like each other and be the same thing: $2(x + 3)$ and $2x + 6$ give the same answer for every value of $x$. Expanding and simplifying are the two directions of travel between such forms, and what makes them worth anything is the rule that the value never changes — only the appearance does.

That matters because the appearance is what you can see. One arrangement hides the answer, another makes it obvious, and only one of them can be solved. Rewriting an expression while being sure you have not altered it is the move every later piece of algebra stands on.

examples.title: The trick that always ends on 1
examples.body:
Think of a number. Add 3. Double it. Take away 4. Halve it. Now subtract the number you first thought of. You have 1, and so has everyone else in the room.

Try it with 7 and you get 1. Try it with 2.5 and you get 1. That is evidence, and evidence cannot tell you whether some number somewhere breaks it. Expanding can: $2(n + 3) - 4 = 2n + 2$, halved is $n + 1$, and $n + 1 - n = 1$.

The $n$ cancels, so the number you started with was never in the answer — which is why the trick cannot fail. Every one of these is built the same way, as a chain of operations arranged to make the variable disappear, and expanding the chain is how you both see through one and design one.

examples.title: A rise and a fall that do not cancel
examples.body:
A price goes up by 10% and later comes down by 10%. Most people expect to be back where they started. Multiply instead: $\times 1.1$ then $\times 0.9$ is $\times 0.99$. A penny in the pound has gone, and it goes in whichever order the two changes happen.

The general case is a two-bracket expansion, and it is the one worth knowing on sight: $(1 + r)(1 - r) = 1 - r^2$. The middle terms $+r$ and $-r$ cancel. The $r^2$ does not, and that leftover square **is** the loss.

Because it is a square it grows fast. Up and down 10% costs 1p in the pound. Up and down 20% costs 4p. Up and down 50% — a half-price sale after a half-price rise — costs 25p, a quarter of the money, from two changes that sound as though they undo each other.

examples.title: Squaring in your head
examples.body:
$97^2$ looks like a job for a calculator. Written as $(100 - 3)^2$ it is not: expanding gives $100^2 - 2 \times 100 \times 3 + 3^2 = 10\,000 - 600 + 9 = 9409$, and every one of those is a step you can take while walking.

The same move handles a product. $32 \times 28$ is $(30 + 2)(30 - 2)$, the middle terms cancel exactly as before, and what is left is $900 - 4 = 896$. $19 \times 7$ is $20 \times 7 - 7 = 133$, which is the same idea with one bracket.

Expanding brackets is taught as something done to an algebraic expression. It is older and more ordinary than that: it is the rule that lets you swap an awkward number for a convenient one and a correction.

steps.title: Terms, and collecting like ones
steps.body:
**An expression is built from terms.** In $7x - 4x + 2$ there are three terms: $+7x$, $-4x$ and $+2$.

**Read each sign as belonging to the term after it.** That habit removes most sign errors before they happen — the $-$ is part of $-4x$, not an instruction floating between terms.

**Like terms have the same letter raised to the same power.** Only like terms can be collected:

- $3x$ and $5x$ — **like**, so $3x + 5x = 8x$
- $3x$ and $3x^2$ — **not like**: same letter, different power
- $3x$ and $3y$ — **not like**: different letters
- $4xy$ and $7xy$ — **like**, so they collect to $11xy$
- $4xy$ and $4x$ — **not like**

**So $x^2 + x$ cannot be simplified.** It is already as simple as it gets, and writing $2x^2$ or $2x$ is a real error rather than a shortcut. Questions are set to test exactly this.

**The notation the spec expects** is worth stating: write $ab$ rather than $a \times b$, $3y$ rather than $y + y + y$, $a^2$ rather than $a \times a$, and $\dfrac{a}{b}$ rather than $a \div b$. These are conventions, but marks depend on using them.

steps.title: Expanding a single bracket
steps.body:
**To expand a bracket, multiply every term inside it by the term outside.**

$$a(b + c) = ab + ac$$

**Every** term, not just the first. Writing the two products on their own line before adding them costs one extra line and removes the commonest error in the topic.

steps.title: Expanding two brackets
steps.body:
**Every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second.** For two brackets of two terms each, that is **four** products.

$$(x + p)(x + q) = x^2 + px + qx + pq = x^2 + (p + q)x + pq$$

A useful check falls out of that last form: **the $x$ coefficient is the sum of the two numbers, and the constant is their product.**

steps.title: Factorising: expanding backwards
steps.body:
**Factorising puts the brackets back.** You look for what every term has in common and take it outside.

**Find the highest common factor of the terms**, then divide each term by it:

$$12x + 20 = 4(3x + 5)$$

Here the HCF of $12$ and $20$ is $4$. Dividing gives $3x$ and $5$, which go inside.

**It must be the *highest* common factor.** $12x + 20 = 2(6x + 10)$ is true, but it is **not fully factorised** — a 2 can still come out of the bracket. A question saying *factorise fully* is testing exactly that.

**Letters count too.** In $6x^2 + 9x$, every term has a 3 and an $x$, so the HCF is $3x$ and the answer is $3x(2x + 3)$.

**Always expand back to check.** $4(3x + 5) = 12x + 20$ ✓. That check is free, takes one line, and catches both a wrong factor and a sign error — which is why it is worth doing every time.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Simplify $7x - 4x + 2$.
2. Expand $5(2x + 3)$.
3. Can $x^2 + x$ be simplified? Explain.

**Part B.**

4. Expand and simplify $4(2x + 1) - 3(x - 2)$.
5. Expand $(x + 2)(x + 6)$.
6. Factorise fully $12x + 20$.

**Part C.**

7. Expand $(x + 5)(x - 2)$, and check your answer by substituting $x = 1$.
8. Factorise fully $6x^2 + 9x$, and show your answer is right by expanding it back.
9. A student writes $12x + 20 = 2(6x + 10)$. Explain why this does not fully answer *factorise fully*.

For question 4, be careful with the sign in front of the second bracket.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Substitution is the check that actually works.** Rereading an expansion tends to repeat the original mistake, because you read what you meant to write. Putting $x = 2$ into the original and into your answer compares them as **numbers**, which is independent of how you got there. Avoid $x = 0$, which hides every $x$ term, and $x = 1$, which makes coefficients indistinguishable from each other.

**Attach every sign to the term that follows it.** In $4(2x + 1) - 3(x - 2)$ the second bracket is multiplied by $-3$, not 3, so the last product is $-3 \times -2 = +6$. Writing the $-3$ deliberately and then multiplying is more reliable than expanding with 3 and trying to flip the signs afterwards.

**Not everything simplifies.** $x^2 + x$ is finished. So is $3x + 2y$. Examiners set these because the instinct to combine is strong, and a wrong simplification is worse than none — it changes the expression rather than tidying it.

**Fully means fully.** $2(6x + 10)$ is a correct factorisation and a wrong answer to *factorise fully*, because a further 2 comes out. Take the **highest** common factor, including any letters: in $6x^2 + 9x$ that is $3x$, not 3.

**The sum-and-product pattern is worth recognising on sight.** In $(x + p)(x + q)$ the $x$ coefficient is $p + q$ and the constant is $pq$. That makes expanding quicker, and it is the same relationship you will run backwards when factorising quadratics — so time spent on it here is repaid later.

**And expanding back is not optional when factorising.** It is the only check that tests both the factor and the signs at once, and it takes a single line. A factorisation offered without it is a guess with good handwriting.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An expression is built from **terms**, and each **sign belongs to the term after it**.
- **Like terms** have the **same letter to the same power**, and only like terms can be collected.
- $3x$ and $3x^2$ are **not** like terms; nor are $3x$ and $3y$.
- So **$x^2 + x$ cannot be simplified** — writing $2x$ or $2x^2$ is an error, not a shortcut.
- Notation: write $ab$, $3y$, $a^2$ and $\dfrac{a}{b}$ rather than the long forms.
- **Expanding a bracket**: $a(b + c) = ab + ac$ — the outside term multiplies **every** term inside.
- A **negative** outside the bracket changes the sign of **both** products.
- **Two brackets** give **four** products: $(x + p)(x + q) = x^2 + (p + q)x + pq$.
- So the **$x$ coefficient is the sum** and the **constant is the product**.
- **Factorising** is expanding backwards: take out the **highest common factor**.
- The factor may include a **letter**: $6x^2 + 9x = 3x(2x + 3)$.
- *Factorise fully* means the bracket must have **no common factor left**.
- **Check an expansion by substituting** a number into both the original and the answer.
- Avoid $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, which hide too much.
- **Check a factorisation by expanding it back** — it tests the factor and the signs at once.

questions.prompt: Explain what like terms are, why $x^2 + x$ cannot be simplified, and how to expand and simplify $4(2x + 1) - 3(x - 2)$.
questions.solution:
**Like terms** are terms with the **same letter raised to the same power**. $3x$ and $5x$ are like terms and collect to $8x$; $4xy$ and $7xy$ collect to $11xy$. Terms that differ in either respect are not like terms: $3x$ and $3y$ have different letters, and $3x$ and $3x^2$ have the same letter to different powers.

That is why **$x^2 + x$ cannot be simplified**. It is tempting to write $2x$ or $2x^2$, but neither is the same expression. Substituting $x = 3$ settles it: the original is $9 + 3 = 12$, while $2x$ would be $6$ and $2x^2$ would be $18$. The expression is already in its simplest form, and writing anything else **changes** it rather than tidying it.

To expand and simplify $4(2x + 1) - 3(x - 2)$, take one bracket at a time.

The first bracket is multiplied by $4$: $4 \times 2x = 8x$ and $4 \times 1 = 4$, giving $8x + 4$.

The second bracket is multiplied by **$-3$**, not 3 — the sign belongs to the term that follows it. So $-3 \times x = -3x$, and $-3 \times -2 = \mathbf{+6}$, because a negative times a negative is positive. That gives $-3x + 6$. This is the step where marks are most often lost: expanding with 3 and trying to flip the signs afterwards is far less reliable than attaching the minus first.

Putting the two together: $8x + 4 - 3x + 6$.

Now **collect like terms**, keeping the $x$ terms and the numbers separate: $8x - 3x = 5x$, and $4 + 6 = 10$. The answer is $\mathbf{5x + 10}$.

It is worth checking by **substitution**, because rereading algebra tends to repeat the original error. Putting $x = 2$ into the original gives $4(5) - 3(0) = 20$, and into the answer gives $5(2) + 10 = 20$. They agree, so the expansion is right.

questions.prompt: Explain how to factorise an expression fully, why "fully" matters, and how you would check your answer. Use $12x + 20$ and $6x^2 + 9x$ as examples.
questions.solution:
**Factorising is expanding backwards.** Instead of multiplying out a bracket, you look for what all the terms have in common and take it outside one.

For **$12x + 20$**, ask what divides both terms. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 and of 20 are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, so the **highest common factor is 4**. Dividing each term by 4 gives $3x$ and $5$, which go inside: $\mathbf{4(3x + 5)}$.

The word **fully** is doing real work in the question. $2(6x + 10)$ is a perfectly **true** statement — expanding it does return $12x + 20$ — but it is **not fully factorised**, because $6x$ and $10$ still share a factor of 2 that could come out. An answer is fully factorised only when the terms inside the bracket have **nothing left in common**. In $4(3x + 5)$, the $3x$ and the $5$ share no factor, so it is finished.

The common factor can include a **letter** as well as a number, and this is the case most often missed. In **$6x^2 + 9x$**, both terms are divisible by 3, and both contain at least one $x$. So the highest common factor is **$3x$**, not 3. Dividing gives $2x$ and $3$, so the answer is $\mathbf{3x(2x + 3)}$. Taking out only 3 would give $3(2x^2 + 3x)$, which is true but leaves an $x$ common inside — not full.

**Always check by expanding back.** For the first: $4 \times 3x = 12x$ and $4 \times 5 = 20$, which returns the original. For the second: $3x \times 2x = 6x^2$ and $3x \times 3 = 9x$ ✓.

That check is worth doing every time, for two reasons. It costs a single line, and it tests **two things at once** — whether the factor taken out was right, and whether the signs inside are right. A factorisation offered without it is really a guess; with it, you know.

examTechnique.body:
Two instincts to resist. The first is combining terms that are not **like** — $x^2 + x$ is finished, and so is $3x + 2y$. The second is expanding a bracket and forgetting the second term, or losing a sign in front of it.

Both are caught by the same habit: **substitute a number**. Put $x = 2$ into the original and into your answer and compare. It takes seconds, works on every expansion, and is independent of the working that produced the error.
examinerErrors: Simplifying $x^2 + x$ to $2x$ or $2x^2$, when it cannot be simplified at all.
Multiplying only the **first** term inside a bracket: $3(2x + 5) = 6x + 5$.
Getting the sign wrong after a negative bracket: $-3(x - 2) = -3x - 6$ instead of $-3x + 6$.
Answering *factorise fully* with a **common** rather than the **highest common** factor.
Forgetting that a common factor may include a **letter**, as in $3x(2x + 3)$.
Swapping the **sum** and the **product** when expanding two brackets.
Writing $a \times b$ or $a \div b$ rather than $ab$ and $\dfrac{a}{b}$.
Checking by rereading, which repeats the original mistake, instead of substituting.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer knows when an expression is **already finished** and says so rather than forcing a simplification. It attaches every **sign to the term after it**, so a negative bracket is expanded with the minus included instead of corrected afterwards. It reads $(x + p)(x + q)$ as **sum and product** and can run that backwards. It treats *fully* as a real instruction, taking out the **highest** common factor including any letter. And it checks — **substituting** a value into an expansion, **expanding back** a factorisation — knowing that rereading algebra mostly repeats the error that was made.
